short: A meridian arc forty metres high, and the best star positions measured before the telescope.
full:
Built at Samarkand between 1424 and 1429, the observatory was a cylindrical building some forty-six metres across and three storeys high on a hill above the city. Its main instrument was the Fakhri sextant, a marble-faced arc of about forty metres' radius set in the plane of the meridian, its lower portion sunk in a trench cut through the rock so that the whole curve could be used. Scale divisions of seventy centimetres to the degree let the transit of the sun and the brighter stars be read to a precision no earlier instrument had reached. Some sixty astronomers and mathematicians worked there.

Its product was the Zij-i Sultani, issued in 1437 and revised until 1449: the first substantial star catalogue compiled from new observation since Ptolemy, and accurate enough that European astronomers were still consulting it in the seventeenth century, when Thomas Hyde printed the tables at Oxford in 1665. The building itself was pulled down after Ulugh Beg's murder and its site forgotten until the Russian archaeologist Vasily Vyatkin found the buried section of the sextant in 1908.
